references.text: Before the fall, God had not yet caused the plants of the field (עֵשֶׂב הַשָּׂדֶה) to grow, the same expression used in Gen 3:18 regarding what humans must now eat as part of the curse.
The context of 3:18: The Lord curses the ground because of human sin and says that with toil humans shall eat from it all their days.
Continuation of the punishment: By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, until you return to the ground.
Isaiah prophesies about the Lord's vineyard that will be destroyed and overgrown with thorns and thistles, a parallel to the consequences of the curse in Gen 3:18.
Instead of thorns, cypress shall grow up, and instead of nettles, myrtle shall grow up—a prophetic reversal of the curse involving thorns and thistles from Gen 3:18.
Hosea prophesies that thorns and thistles (קוֹץ וְדַרְדַּר) will grow over their altars—the same word pair as in Gen 3:18, the only other place in the OT where both words appear together.
The Hebrews use the image of ground that bears thorns and thistles (ἀκάνθας καὶ τριβόλους) and is near to being cursed, a clear allusion to the curse in Gen 3:17-18.
'And there shall no longer be any curse'—a complete removal of the curse pronounced in Eden, including the thorns and thistles from Gen 3:18.
Isaiah uses the thorns and thistles from Genesis 3:18 as an image of God's judgment and destruction.
Isaiah uses the thorns and thistles from Genesis 3:18 as an image of God's judgment over His own people.
Genesis 6:11 shows the escalating consequence of sin that began with thorns and thistles in 3:18.
Romans 5:12 gives the theological explanation for why thorns and thistles (3:18) exist: sin entered through one man.
